name: DeepSeek Harness + V4-Flash — DeepSeek's own agent runtime on your GPUs
description: DeepSeek's agent harness, running DeepSeek's own frontier open-weight model, on the GPUs you rented — nothing in the loop belongs to anyone else. dsh (DeepSeek Harness) is the agent runtime DeepSeek open-sourced under MIT: a browser UI where the agent reads files, greps, edits, runs commands and shows you its work, with an architecture in which the model adapter, the tool registry, the session log and the agent loop are all replaceable plugins. Next to it in this container, vLLM serves DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 — 284 billion parameters total but only about 13 billion active per token, which is how a model this large answers at agent speed, and 82.7 on Terminal-Bench 2.1. The three deepseek_v4 flags that make this an agent runtime rather than a chat window are wired up: the V4 tokenizer mode (the checkpoint ships encoding scripts instead of a chat template, so this is what makes the OpenAI-compatible endpoint work at all), the V4 tool-call parser and the V4 reasoning parser. Without the parsers the model's tool calls arrive buried in prose and the harness cannot act on a single one, so the launch script proves a real tool call round-trips before the service is ever published. Context here is 393216 tokens rather than the model's full 1048576, because that is the smallest window in which the model's Think Max reasoning effort does not truncate; raise it with VLLM_MAX_MODEL_LEN if your cards have room. SKILLS ARE INCLUDED AND ARE THE POINT: dsh reads the same SKILL.md format and the same discovery roots as every other skills-aware agent, and this bundle installs six skills that a fresh session cannot infer and gets wrong expensively — what survives a container stop and what does not, how to reach and interrogate the local model, why the VRAM is already spent and nothing else may touch it, git-first discipline in a bucket-backed workspace, how ocean-node service templates and bundles are authored, and where the real dsh plugin API lives (pointers only, because the harness is a preview whose API moves). They sit at discovery tier 400 and are rewritten on every launch, so your own skills go in the workspace at .agents/skills, where they outrank them and survive. HOW IT IS PUT TOGETHER: one container, one payment. vLLM binds 127.0.0.1 only, so the raw OpenAI-compatible API is never published and there is no unauthenticated inference endpoint to find. dsh also binds 127.0.0.1 — and here is the part to read twice, because it is the one place this template departs from upstream. DEEPSEEK HARNESS SHIPS NO AUTHENTICATION: its own documentation states the web server has no TLS, no auth and no origin policy, and its agent runs shell commands and writes files in this container, so a public bind would be remote code execution by design and there is no password flag to turn on. The single published port is therefore a Caddy reverse proxy that demands HTTP basic auth before anything reaches dsh. That proxy is this template's addition, not an official DeepSeek deployment pattern — upstream documents no supported way to expose dsh to a network. The connection is plain HTTP because the node publishes a plain TCP port, so the password and everything the agent shows you cross the network in cleartext: use a fresh password per launch, put TLS in front if your node does not, and understand that the container boundary rather than the password is the real isolation. TWO REQUIREMENTS AT LAUNCH, both enforced by the startup script rather than discovered later. First, set DSH_WEB_PASSWORD (12+ characters); the container refuses to start without it. Second, select a persistent-storage bucket. It holds four things that make relaunching cheap: the 166.9 GB of weights, the Node runtime and the pinned dsh release, dsh's settings and session history, and — the one that matters most — /data/outputs/workspace-dsv4, the project directory the agent edits, initialised as a git repository. The node builds a fresh container on every launch, so without a bucket the weights re-download inside your paid window and the code the agent wrote is destroyed on stop; the container refuses to start rather than let that happen. Bring code in and take it out through the bucket. FIRST LAUNCH IS SLOW AND THAT TIME IS BILLED: 166.9 GB from Hugging Face before the model can load, roughly twenty to thirty minutes on a gigabit link. Every launch after that reads it from your bucket. WHAT IS PINNED: the image is vllm/vllm-openai:v0.27.1, dsh is 0.1.1-rc.2 and Caddy 2.11.4, all overridable per launch — dsh is a developer preview whose own README promises compatibility-breaking changes and whose every published version is a release candidate, which is exactly why nothing here resolves "latest" inside a paid window. ONE HONEST CAVEAT, stated because finding it yourself would cost a window: vLLM's own recipe for this checkpoint documents H200-class Hopper cards only under a prefill/decode-disaggregated deployment, and the expert weights are in an fp4 format native to Blackwell. That plain tensor parallelism on Hopper serves this model is this template's single unverified assumption. It is also the reason the script sends one real request, with a tool call, before publishing anything: if the assumption is wrong you learn it from a log line in seconds, not from a silent agent an hour in.
outcome: Open a browser and put DeepSeek's own agent runtime, driven by DeepSeek's own 284B open-weight model on your own GPUs, to work on a persistent git workspace — with a skills library that already knows how this box works.

This entry exists so the launch wizard offers the bucket picker: nodes-dashboard gates that picker on workflows[].length > 0 (templateNeedsBucketPicker in src/services/template-launch.ts). The bucket holds the 166.9 GB of weights, the Node runtime and pinned dsh release, dsh's settings and session history, and the git workspace the agent edits — without it the container refuses to start. The graph is deliberately empty and the container ignores COMFY_WORKFLOW entirely. Delete this once the node exposes a declarative persistence field.

requiredResources.description: At least TWO CUDA GPUs of the 141 GB H200 class, on one host, ideally NVLink-connected. Two is a floor derived from arithmetic, not a preference: the checkpoint is 166.9 GB (its own model.safetensors.index.json), so no single 141 GB card holds it and there is no single-GPU fallback to degrade to. At tensor-parallel size 2 each card holds about 83.5 GB of weights, leaving roughly 43 GB per card for KV cache and activations at 0.90 utilisation — ample for the 393216-token default window, which is an estimated ~17 GB of FP8 KV cache. Four cards are recommended because they double that headroom and put the model's full 1048576-token context within reach via VLLM_MAX_MODEL_LEN — and because of one risk two cards cannot absorb: the experts are stored in fp4, a Blackwell-native format, so a Hopper path that cannot consume it packed would upcast on load, doubling the 155.4 GiB footprint at fp8 or quadrupling it at bf16. Two cards (280 GiB) hold neither; four hold the fp8 case comfortably. That failure appears as a CUDA out-of-memory while loading weights, and the launch script says so and names VLLM_TP_SIZE as the fix. Legal values for VLLM_TP_SIZE are 2, 4 and 8 and nothing else: tensor parallelism splits by whole attention heads and the model has 64, so 6 is arithmetically illegal and vLLM will refuse to start — do not set it to 6 in order to 'use all six cards'. ONE OPERATOR PREREQUISITE, and it is unavoidable here rather than optional: because tensor parallelism is mandatory, vLLM runs one worker process per card and those processes exchange tensors through POSIX shared memory, so the container needs far more than Docker's default 64 MB /dev/shm. The node operator sets this once per GPU resource via init.advanced (ShmSize, optionally IpcMode, PidsLimit) — see docs/compute.md, 'Multi-GPU workloads'. The launch script checks for it before the download starts and exits with an explanatory log line rather than hanging a rendezvous while billing. THE UNVERIFIED PART, stated plainly: vLLM's published recipe for this checkpoint lists H200 only under a prefill/decode-disaggregated deployment, and the expert weights use an fp4 format native to Blackwell. Plain tensor parallelism on Hopper is therefore expected to work but is not documented upstream as a supported layout, which is why the script sends one real request including a tool call before publishing the service — a wrong assumption costs seconds and a log line instead of a paid window. dsh and the auth proxy run on the CPU with CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES emptied, so nothing competes with the model for VRAM.
